children: Global investment company SoftBank Group is seeking a record amount from junk bond investors. It will expand the footprint of artificial intelligence in the speculative-grade world.

Japan's SoftBank Group- a big investor in companies like Arm Holdings, a chip designer- is issuing over $11 billion in junk-rated bonds, according to media reports. Such bonds are riskier, but offer juicy yields. SoftBank's ask surpasses issuance from Luxembourg-based media company Numericable Group, which in 2014 sold a record $10.9 billion in junk bonds globally, per data from LSEG.

SoftBank's deal may price on Thursday, Bloomberg has said, and part of the cash will be used to fund a follow-on investment in the ChatGPT maker OpenAI. It will add to the $4.6 billion SoftBank has already issued this year across two deals. SoftBank sold $7.35 billion in a 2021 deal and that used to be its largest ever bond offering, LSEG data show.

Things are different now. AI is a bigger story in the junk world. Companies were able to get $36 billion to fund their AI buildout this year, more than double the $17 billion in all of 2025, according to Citi data at the end of July. AI fundraising made up 24% of all second-quarter junk bond issuance versus a modest 6% in the second quarter a year ago.

The increasing AI-earmarked junk bond supply is a new phenomenon. In the years prior, much of the cash needed to build data centers has come from free cash on balance sheets, money raised from public equity, and the investment-grade bond market, a corporate debt market reserved for the world's most financially stable companies.

SoftBank's newest mammoth bond sale cements junk debt's status as a funding engine. It tells investors that the demand for AI infrastructure is so vast that virtually no corner of the U.S. capital market remains untouched by AI.

The Japanese group, led by CEO Masayoshi Son, can afford the debt bill. According to ratings agency Fitch, SoftBank is expected to maintain adequate liquidity, with cash covering bond redemptions for at least the next two years. The gross loan-to-value (LTV) ratio- measuring amount borrowed versus value of assets-was around 20% as of June-end under the "less than 25%" established as a policy by SoftBank in 2019.

The LTV is being maintained despite more debt because of the growing value of its holdings, like Arm whose stock is up 195% this year. But SoftBank will have to make some hard decisions, like sell assets, if the AI boom collapses, a European junk bond manager, familiar with the SoftBank planning, told Barron's. "You need to remember that these are lofty valuations."
SoftBank didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Demand for newly issued junk bonds has been weak. As of Sept. 18, yields on new issues were around 8.03%, highest in at least year, according to KDP High Yield New Issues Index.
Slightly over a billion of SoftBank's new debt will be denominated in euros and the rest, or $10 billion, will be in dollars, per media reports.

For high-yield investors, people used to dabbling in treacherous waters, things are getting trickier as AI debt grows. Still, before running for the hills, investors must remember that AI junk debt is still a small portion of the overall market compared to the proportions seen in the stock market and the investment-grade market.
What will be more concerning is if this riskier AI portion keeps growing the next few years.
